summary.text: The Age of Revolution was a period from the late 18th to the mid-19th centuries when many revolutionary movements arose across most of Europe and the Americas.
It is noted for the shift from absolutist monarchies to representative governments with a written constitution, and for the creation of nation states.
The revolutionaries in different countries knew of each other, and to some degree were inspired by or copied each other.

items.prompt: Before this era, many states were ruled by a monarch with unchecked power. What did the era's revolutionaries push toward instead?

options.label: Rule by a single general with lifetime powers
Representative governments with a written constitution
A return to rule by aristocracies and established churches
Direct rule by village assemblies in each region

items.explain: The period is noted for the change from absolutist monarchies to representative governments with a written constitution.

items.prompt: Napoleon's armies brought a civil code and equality before the law to lands they conquered. How did people there often react to his occupation?

options.label: They accepted it gladly, since the reforms were modern
They formed the Holy Alliance to resist him
National rebellions, notably in Spain and Germany
They copied his rule and made themselves emperors

items.explain: His rigorous military occupation triggered national rebellions, notably in Spain and Germany, despite the modern concepts he imposed.

items.prompt: In 1830 and 1848, revolutionaries demanded democracy in places like Italy and Poland. What did those demands often merge with?

options.label: Efforts to restore the old absolutist monarchies
Campaigns to expand each empire's overseas colonies
Demands to give established churches more power
Independence or national unification movements

items.explain: The democratic demands often merged with independence or national unification movements, such as in Italy, Germany, Poland and Hungary.

items.prompt: Around 1810 to 1820, almost all of a European kingdom's American colonies declared independence. What made that possible?

options.label: Wars in Europe left their ruler too weak to control them
The Congress of Vienna granted each colony independence
Their ruler chose to hand over power to the colonists
A revolution at home had overthrown their king

items.explain: Spain was considerably weakened by the Napoleonic Wars and could not control its American colonies, almost all of which proclaimed independence between 1810 and 1820.

items.prompt: Edmund Burke backed the American colonists in 1774 but deplored the French revolutionaries in 1790. What idea guided both positions?

options.label: That the right to own property is essential to freedom
That every monarchy should be overthrown by force
That only nobles deserve a say in government
That equality before the law outweighs every other right

items.explain: In both cases he followed Montesquieu's theory that the right to own property is an essential element of personal freedom.

items.prompt: Looking back, what did the success of these revolutions show?

options.label: That absolutist monarchies were the most stable way to rule
That revolutions only work when great powers approve them
That written constitutions cannot survive a military occupation
That a radically new government could be set up by popular insurgence

items.explain: Their success demonstrated that establishing a radically new government via popular insurgence could work in practice.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The label was made popular by the British historian Eric Hobsbawm. He used it in his 1962 book The Age of Revolution: Europe 1789–1848. Revolutions in this period struck the United States, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, France, Haiti, Ireland and Spanish America, with smaller upheavals in Switzerland, Russia and Brazil. The rebels in these places knew about one another, and to some extent they took inspiration from or copied each other.

paragraphs.heading: From America to France
paragraphs.text: Shaped by the new thinking of the Enlightenment, the American Revolution of 1765–1783 is usually treated as the opening event. France, the Netherlands and Spain helped the new United States win its independence from Britain. The French Revolution followed in 1789, and its wars carried it quickly across Europe. After Napoleon seized power in 1799, he conquered most of the continent and brought ideas such as equality before the law and a civil code, but his harsh occupation sparked national revolts, notably in Spain and Germany.

paragraphs.heading: The Americas break free
paragraphs.text: Haiti's revolution broke out in the 1790s and lasted until 1804. Spain came out of the Napoleonic Wars badly weakened and could no longer hold its American colonies. Almost all of them declared independence between 1810 and 1820, and Colombia was among the first South American nations to do so. With Spain caught up in European wars, its mainland colonies won their independence around 1820.

paragraphs.heading: Waves across Europe
paragraphs.text: Once Napoleon was beaten, the great powers of Europe met at the Congress of Vienna in 1814–15 and forged the Holy Alliance, hoping to stop future revolutions, and they put the old monarchies back. Even so, revolt returned to southern Europe in 1820, in Portugal, Spain, Italy and Greece. Two more similar waves shook the continent, in 1830 and in 1848, also known as the Spring of Nations. Demands for democracy often blended with drives for independence or national unity, as in Italy, Germany, Poland and Hungary, and the violent crushing of the Spring of Nations closed the era.

paragraphs.heading: What the revolutions left
paragraphs.text: Seen over the long run, the revolutions mostly succeeded. They spread far and wide the ideals of liberalism and republicanism, along with the idea of overthrowing aristocracies, kings and state churches. Their success showed that a revolution in the modern sense, setting up a radically new government through a popular uprising, could actually work. Revolutionary movements and ideas have existed ever since.

paragraphs.heading: Burke's two verdicts
paragraphs.text: The writings of Edmund Burke weaken the picture of one shared Atlantic story. In 1774 he backed the American colonists, arguing that the crown was taking their property and rights without consent. In 1790 he condemned the French Revolution, because there the revolutionaries themselves were stripping away property, customary and religious rights. In both cases he followed Montesquieu's view that owning property is a core part of personal freedom.
